passage: Omkar, I've decided. Hemant is officially skipping the school trip to Mahabaleshwar. Don't laugh. Have you seen how many bus accidents there are? Every night my feed shows me another one: a bus hanging off a ghat road, a truck on fire, people crying at the roadside. Yesterday I watched maybe twenty clips. Twenty, Omkar! Buses are basically death boxes now. My dad says he's done that road a hundred times and it's fine, but he doesn't see what I see. And the city isn't any better. There were three videos of bikes crashing at signals just this week. Honestly, I don't know how anyone goes anywhere. I'll stay home and look at the trip photos. Safer.

qa.a: Hemant watched maybe twenty clips.

qa.q: Why does bus travel feel so dangerous to Hemant?
qa.a: Seeing crash after crash every night makes accidents feel common, so the number of clips feels like the number of real crashes. Dad's hundred safe trips feel less real than the videos.

qa.q: What could help Hemant check the real risk before skipping the trip?
qa.a: Hemant could ask how many school trips on that road had problems, find out how many buses travel it safely every day, and take a break from the clips for a week.

qa.a: Omkar may worry about Hemant and feel disappointed about the trip, and might notice that the clips, not the road, have changed the plan.

passage: I'm Afreen, Zubin's older sister, and lately I've watched my brother change. He's fifteen, and he used to cycle everywhere. At dinner he told Abbu the city was "the most dangerous place on earth" and listed four accidents he'd seen that week: one in Jaipur, two abroad, one he couldn't place. Abbu said he'd driven here for thirty years without a scratch. Zubin just shook his head. I don't know if he's really scared or just caught up in those videos, but his cycle hasn't moved in a month.

qa.a: Zubin listed four accidents he'd seen that week.

qa.q: What does Zubin's head shake at Abbu's answer suggest?
qa.a: It suggests the reels feel more convincing to him than Abbu's thirty years of safe driving; seeing crashes every night has made danger feel everywhere.

qa.q: How could Afreen help Zubin get back on his cycle?
qa.a: Afreen could point out with him that the four crashes came from far-off places, suggest a short break from the reels, and ride a familiar route with him to rebuild confidence.

qa.a: Afreen seems worried and a bit helpless, watching her brother's world shrink without knowing how scared he truly is.

You wouldn't take the shared auto to tuition. You wanted your abbu to drive you, both ways, every day. I asked you, "How many of your friends have been in an accident?" You said, "Nani, you don't understand, I see it every day." And that was it, you see? You saw it every day, on the phone. Not on the road. Your abbu and I, we've taken autos for thirty years. Then your teacher showed your class real road figures for our district, and your face changed. You took the auto the next Monday, holding my hand very tight.

passage: The application for the summer science programme in Mumbai closed at midnight, and at 10:40 Farida still hadn't pressed submit. The power had gone at nine, and her laptop was at 14 percent. Nandini sat beside her with a torch. "What's the problem? You've wanted this all year." Farida scrolled on her phone instead. "Look. People packed on local trains. Someone falling off at a station. A building collapse. Floods. My feed is full of it. Mumbai is just unsafe." "How many of those clips are from this year?" "I don't know. Lots." "My cousin lived there two years," Nandini said. "She took the train daily. The worst thing that happened was a stolen umbrella." Farida went quiet. "It feels like it happens every day." "It happens every day on your phone." At 11:52, the laptop at 4 percent, Farida pressed submit.

qa.a: It closed at midnight.

qa.q: Why does Mumbai feel "just unsafe" to Farida?
qa.a: Her feed is full of dramatic clips about trains, collapses and floods, so it feels like these things happen constantly. Seeing them often is mistaken for them being common.

qa.q: With the battery running out, what helped Farida make her choice?
qa.a: Nandini asked how many clips were recent and shared her cousin's real experience of daily train travel. Comparing the feed with an actual life gave Farida enough balance to press submit.

"Uday, you've watched twenty crashes this morning. How many have you seen with your own eyes in our lane?" Uday scrolled, frowning. "None. But that's because I stopped cycling." passage: In Class 9, I stopped cycling to school. I told my parents it was because of the sun. The real reason was the reels. Every night I scrolled through videos of road accidents: a scooter flipping, a truck swerving, a cyclist on a highway. After a while my feed was nothing but crashes. I became sure the roads of Nashik were a war zone. My friend Damini, who cycled with me every day for two years, kept asking why. I said, "Don't you watch the news?" She said, "Irawati, we've done this route five hundred times. Nothing happened." I didn't listen. I took the auto, which was actually more crowded and honestly more scary. Looking back, I think I mixed up how often I saw accidents with how often they happened.

qa.q: What did Irawati take instead of cycling?
qa.a: The auto.

qa.q: Why did the roads feel like a war zone to Irawati?
qa.a: Watching crash videos every night made accidents feel constant, so Irawati felt scared even though the real route had been safe for years.

qa.q: What could Irawati have done to check the fear?
qa.a: Irawati could have compared the five hundred safe rides with the videos, or looked up real local accident figures with a parent.

qa.q: How might Damini have felt cycling alone after Irawati stopped?
qa.a: Damini may have felt lonely and puzzled, missing a cycling friend and not understanding the fear.

passage:
Class 10 counsellor's note, Thursday

Jyoti came to see me today because she wants to skip the school's bus trip to the science museum next week. She said, "Buses crash all the time. I see it every day." When I asked where, she showed me her phone: clip after clip of bus accidents, most from other countries, some years old.

She was clearly frightened, her hands cold. I didn't laugh or argue. I asked her how many school trips she'd been on. About twelve. How many had problems? None. Then we looked together at how the app decides what to show her. She was surprised that watching one crash had filled her feed.

She has agreed to think about going and to take a break from those videos this week. I'll check in with her on Monday.

— Jagdish

qa.q: How many school trips had Jyoti been on?
qa.a: About twelve.

qa.q: Why was Jyoti so frightened of the bus trip?
qa.a: Seeing crash clips every day made bus accidents feel constant, so she felt frightened even though her real trips had been safe.

qa.q: What did Jagdish do that helped Jyoti?
qa.a: Jagdish stayed calm, compared her real trips with the clips, and showed her how the app fills the feed, helping her see exposure isn't real frequency.

qa.q: How might Jyoti's friends see her wanting to skip the trip?
qa.a: Her friends might be confused or disappointed, not knowing the videos had made her so scared.

grounding: It shows, through a counsellor's note, a teenager whose feed of crash clips makes bus travel seem far riskier than it is.

passage:
Friday night

Didn't sign up for the inter-school fest in Mumbai. Zeenat is going. Everyone is going. I told Ma I had a stomach ache.

The truth: I can't stop watching those videos. Trains packed with people hanging out the doors. A car flipping on the expressway. A bus in the rain. My feed is full of them, maybe twenty a day. Every time I open my phone there's another one.

So in my head, travelling to Mumbai = accident.

Zeenat laughed at me. She said, "Kamal, my Chacha has taken that train every day for eleven years. Nothing happened." I said he was lucky.

But now writing this I'm thinking. Twenty videos a day. From the whole country. Maybe from the whole world. And my feed keeps showing them because I keep watching them.

Maybe the trains aren't more dangerous. Maybe my phone just is.

qa.q: How many accident videos a day does Kamal say the feed shows?
qa.a: Maybe twenty a day.

qa.q: Why does Kamal feel that travelling to Mumbai means an accident?
qa.a: Kamal feels anxious because the feed keeps showing crash videos, so the danger seems everywhere even though the clips come from the whole country.

qa.q: What could Kamal try to get a truer picture of the risk?
qa.a: Kamal could stop watching the clips for a while and ask an adult or look up how many people travel that route safely every day.

qa.q: How might Zeenat see Kamal's decision to skip the fest?
qa.a: Zeenat probably finds it surprising and a bit sad, since her Chacha has taken that train for eleven years without trouble.

grounding: A teenager who watches many viral accident clips believes travel is far riskier than it is and skips a school trip.

passage:
In Rekha's small town near Satara, everyone said she was the brightest girl in Class 11. Her maths teacher had arranged a scholarship at a coaching centre in Pune.

Rekha said no.

Her friend Madhuri found her behind the family's grocery shop, scrolling. "Why?"

Rekha held up the phone. A clip of a crowded Pune road. A chain-snatching caught on camera. A scooter crash at night. "Every day there's something. The city is dangerous."

"How many of these have you watched?"

"Hundreds, maybe."

"And how many girls from our school are studying in Pune right now?"

Rekha counted. Nine. Madhuri's own sister was one of them.

"Has anything happened to any of them?"

"No, but..."

"So hundreds of clips, and nine real girls who are fine."

Rekha put the phone face down on the rice sacks. She still felt the fear in her stomach. But for the first time, she wondered where it had really come from.

qa.q: How many girls from their school were studying in Pune?
qa.a: Nine.

qa.q: Why did Rekha feel the city was so dangerous?
qa.a: Rekha felt afraid because she had watched hundreds of clips of accidents and chain-snatching, so seeing them often felt like they happen often.

qa.q: What could Rekha do before making her final decision?
qa.a: Rekha could talk to the nine girls in Pune, including Madhuri's sister, and discuss real safety steps with her teacher and family.

qa.q: How might Rekha's maths teacher feel about the refusal?
qa.a: The teacher might feel disappointed and worried that a real opportunity is being lost to fear from clips, and want to talk it through.

passage:
It was the Christmas holidays in Lisbon, and Paulo's family planned to drive to his grandparents' village. Paulo, fifteen, didn't want to go.
For weeks his video feed had been full of crash clips: cars sliding on wet roads, pile-ups on motorways, a bus on its side. He had watched dozens. Now every road looked like a disaster waiting.
"We drive there every year," his older brother Mateo said. "Nothing's ever happened."
"You haven't seen the videos."
"I've seen some. They're from all over the world, over years. Of course there are loads."
Paulo shook his head. "It happens all the time. I see it every day."
Mateo held up his own phone. "Because the app keeps showing you what you watch. How many crashes have you actually seen in real life?"
Paulo thought. "None," he admitted, but his stomach still felt tight.

qa.q: How many crashes had Paulo seen in real life?
qa.a: He admitted he had seen none.

qa.q: Why does the road trip feel so dangerous to Paulo?
qa.a: He feels anxious because he has watched dozens of crash clips, so seeing them every day makes crashes feel common in real life.

qa.q: What could help Paulo judge the risk more accurately?
qa.a: He could look at how many trips happen without accidents, and take a break from crash videos so the feed stops filling his head with them.

qa.q: How does Mateo see Paulo's fear?
qa.a: Mateo sees it as a result of the app feeding Paulo more of what he watches, and tries patiently to point out the difference between the feed and real life.
